chem-electrolysis: Electrolysis uses electricity to force a reaction that wouldn't happen on its own — an electric current splits compounds apart. Run current through water and it separates into hydrogen and oxygen gas bubbles; run it through molten salt and you get pure sodium metal. It's how aluminum, chlorine, and many pure elements are made industrially.
chem-electroplating: Electroplating uses electricity to coat one metal with another: dissolve a metal in solution, pass a current through it and an object, and metal ions deposit atom by atom onto the surface. That's how jewelry gets its gold layer, car parts get chrome, and coins get their shine. The coating can be microscopic yet completely change how a surface looks and behaves.
chem-electrochemical-cell: An electrochemical cell is the reverse of electrolysis: instead of forcing a reaction with electricity, it lets a spontaneous reaction produce electricity. Two different metals in a solution, connected by a wire, push electrons from one to the other — that flow is current. Every battery is one or more electrochemical cells, converting chemical energy into the electricity that powers your devices.
chem-lemon-battery: A lemon battery works because two different metals — a zinc nail and a copper coin — push electrons through the lemon's acidic juice. The acid carries ions between them, the metals exchange electrons, and a wire connecting them carries current. One lemon makes only a tiny voltage, but string several together and you can light a small LED — pure electrochemistry from fruit.
chem-voltaic-pile: The first real battery was Alessandro Volta's 1800 pile: alternating discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cardboard, stacked like a coin tower. Each pair generated a small voltage, and the whole stack added up to a usable current. It was the first device to produce steady electricity on demand — and Napoleon was so impressed he made Volta a count.
chem-galvani-frogs: Electrochemistry began with a frog: in the 1780s, Luigi Galvani noticed that dissected frog legs twitched when touched with two different metals. He thought it was 'animal electricity,' but Volta realized the twitch came from the metals themselves — a battery, not a frog. Their debate over who was right built the foundation of electrochemistry, and both names live on in science.
chem-battery-types: A battery stores chemical energy and releases it as electricity when the two electrode reactions connect. In a lithium-ion cell, lithium ions shuttle between electrodes as you charge and discharge; in an alkaline cell, zinc and manganese dioxide react. They all share the same core: an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte, and a wire that forces the electrons to do work on the way.
chem-fuel-cells: A fuel cell is a battery that never dies: feed it hydrogen and oxygen continuously and it produces electricity, with water as its only exhaust. The hydrogen gives up electrons at one electrode; the oxygen accepts them at the other; the electrons flow through the circuit doing work. Fuel cells power spacecraft, buses, and some cars — clean energy that runs as long as fuel flows.
chem-redox-reactions: Redox — reduction-oxidation — is the electron-shuffling chemistry behind batteries, rust, bleach, and breathing. One species loses electrons (oxidized), another gains them (reduced), and the two always happen together. Your cells extract energy from food via a long chain of redox steps, and every rechargeable battery cycles redox reactions thousands of times.
chem-oxidation-numbers: Oxidation numbers are a bookkeeping system for electrons: each atom in a molecule gets a number tracking how many electrons it's gained or lost compared to the free element. Oxygen is almost always -2, hydrogen +1, and pure elements are 0. By tallying these numbers, chemists can see exactly which atoms are oxidized and which are reduced in any reaction.
chem-galvanic-cells: A galvanic cell is a battery in its purest form: two half-cells, each with a metal electrode dipped in its own ion solution, connected by a wire and a salt bridge. One metal dissolves, pushing electrons out; the other accepts them. The voltage between them depends on how badly each metal wants to shed electrons — the reactivity series turned into electricity.
chem-electrode-potentials: Every metal has a characteristic 'want' to give up electrons, measured as an electrode potential. Zinc wants to shed them (negative potential), copper is content to accept them (positive), and the voltage of a cell is simply the difference between the two. This ladder of potentials is why a zinc-copper battery gives about 1.1 volts and why lithium's strong potential makes it so energetic.
chem-nernst-equation: The Nernst equation corrects a battery's voltage for what's actually in solution — concentrations shift the potential, and the equation quantifies exactly how much. It was derived by Walther Nernst in 1889 and earned him the 1920 Nobel Prize. It's why a dying battery reads lower voltage: the reactants have been consumed, and the equation predicts the sag.
chem-corrosion-electrochemistry: Corrosion is electrochemistry gone rogue: a metal like iron acts as a tiny battery, with wet patches as electrodes and dissolved oxygen as the other half of the cell. Electrons flow through the metal itself while ions move through the water, slowly dissolving the iron into rust. It costs the world hundreds of billions of dollars a year in bridges, pipelines, and ships.
chem-sacrificial-anodes: A sacrificial anode is a metal more eager to corrode than the one you're protecting — zinc or magnesium bolted to a steel hull or water heater. Because zinc gives up electrons more readily, the steel becomes the cathode and never rusts; the zinc dissolves instead. Ships, pipelines, and water tanks carry these quietly dying bodyguards, replaced only when they've fully sacrificed themselves.
chem-cathodic-protection: Cathodic protection stops corrosion by making the metal the cathode of an electric circuit so it can't lose electrons. It's done two ways: with sacrificial anodes that corrode instead, or with an impressed current from a power supply that pumps electrons into the structure. Pipelines, storage tanks, and bridge rebar across the world are kept alive by this invisible electric shield.
chem-electroplating-chemistry: Electroplating chemistry is all about the ions in the bath: dissolve gold, silver, or chromium salts in solution, dip the object as the cathode, and metal ions swim to it, gaining electrons and depositing as a smooth layer. Current density and bath temperature control the finish — bright or matte, thick or thin. The same science that plates jewelry also protects steel from rust.
